newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's Van Miert warns on sports broadcasting rules.
newsitem.headline: EU's Van Miert warns on sports broadcasting rules.

text.p: European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said on Thursday he was increasingly concerned about a handful of private media giants using their power to buy exclusive sports broadcasting rights.
He told the European Parliament the commission would insist on allowing the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), a group of public television channels, to negotiate similar rights for its members.

Responding to a challenge by private broadcasters, the European Court of Justice ruled in July that a former commission decision, effectively exempting EBU from competition rules, had not been properly drafted.
But Van Miert said the commission would now re-adopt its decision, bearing in mind the court's ruling.

"We are currently carrying out an in-depth assessment of the court's decision but we think, that as to the substance, there is no reason to change our decision," Van Miert told the European Parliament's economic and monetary committee.
"There is this trend which seriously worries us that increasingly a few large groups can buy such rights."
Van Miert said it seemed only fair that public broadcasters unite to face media tycoons like Rupert Murdoch and Leo Kirch.
In July, Germany's Kirch group won a bidding battle for television rights to the 2002 and 2006 World Cup Soccer Finals.
In his address to parliament, Van Miert, who is an enthusiastic soccer fan, also warned European soccer governing body UEFA about its broadcasting rules.
"We think UEFA conditions are too strict," he said, adding that the commission had received complaints.
"We are in discussions with UEFA, but if there is no progress we will have to act."
Van Miert did not elaborate but commission officials said the complaints were filed by television channels which broadcast UEFA matches but do not have exclusive rights.

Van Miert also made it known he was unhappy with plans by the Dutch football association KNVB to grant seven years of exclusive broadcasting rights to sports channel Sport 7 in which it is a shareholder.
KNVB notified the commission in August of its plans to grant Sports 7 exclusive rights to broadcast Dutch premier league football matches.
"Seven years is too long," Van Miert told the committee.
He hinted the commissison might ask KNVB to reduce the period to five years, as was decided for a similar case involving British TV channel BSkyB.
There is no deadline for the commission to come to a decision on the KNVB case but it usually informs companies of its preliminary finds within two months of notification.
Other shareholders in Sports 7 include powerful Dutch groups Philips Electronics NV, ING NV and publishing company Endemol.
